text: Taeo pressed his thumb into his palm, searching for the pulse. There was nothing. With Nib across the gate, the link had fallen silent.
Inside, Nib stood on a cliffside gallery beneath a lavender sky. A sheer drop waited beyond the old stone supports. Far ahead, white stone streaked the cliff.
Outside, six minutes had passed. Haein worked on the radios, Sejin ate her kimbap, and Taeo stood at the safety tape clutching his log.
Haein tried different radio bands, although none crossed the gate. She knew the rule. She kept trying anyway.
Taeo drifted past the tape without noticing. Haein hooked a finger through his vest and pulled him back without even turning around.
Sejin reminded him that the knock was due at forty minutes, not six. Taeo had called waiting difficult before. He was only now learning what it meant.
Inside, Nib insisted on carrying the long tripod case. His determination lasted longer than his balance. The wooden mule managed its own load considerably better.
Nib surrendered the case and assigned their duties: 'You carry. I look.' Minho approved the arrangement and suggested he start looking.
Nib scouted ahead, reporting loose grit over the radio to Minho. He also pressed his hand against the cliff. Outside, Taeo's palm remained silent.
At twenty minutes, Taeo flinched at another passing train. It was already the fourth. Sejin told him to sit down. He insisted he was fine.
Haein asked why he didn't go in with Nib. Taeo looked toward the gate and said he couldn't. He gave her no further explanation.
Her father had gone first on every job. Now Minho did. Haein returned to her circuit board. She built things so she could help from outside.
Twenty-seven minutes into the survey, Nib stopped near the white outcrop. The mule kept walking until its summoner ordered it to stop. Above them, grit trickled from a hairline crack.
Nib pointed out the damaged strut. Minho couldn't see the crack at first. Nib told him to watch the moving grit. Then Minho saw it.
The outcrop was their final survey station. Minho braced the strut with a steel prop and ordered them through one at a time. The mule would stay behind.
Nib volunteered to go first. He walked alone beneath the damaged support toward the white stone while the others watched from the near side.
Outside, Taeo waited with his fist beside the frame. Haein counted the final ten seconds. The stopwatch reached forty minutes.
Taeo knocked twice, carefully, just as they had agreed. Then all three waited. Nobody came out, and no answer came through.
Taeo decided that if Nib was fine, he would never speak to him again. His jaw stayed clenched, and his eyes never left the gate.
Then the gate shuddered, throwing out grit. Taeo asked whether it was another train. Sejin reached for her medical kit. That sound had come through the gate.
Taeo hammered two more knocks into the steel and split a knuckle. Behind him, Haein stared at the gate over her stopwatch, waiting for her brother.
Before Taeo could knock again, three answering knocks came from inside. Three meant coming. His face broke into something between a laugh and a sob.
Nib stepped out covered in stone dust, his right hand closed around something small. The unused return mark faded as he crossed back into Seoul.
The amber pulse returned to Taeo's palm the moment Nib was back on the same side. He could feel him again.
Nib held up a chalk-white pebble. It was the same kind of stone as the white patch beside his wall. He had found the match he wanted.
Taeo's legs finally gave out, dropping him onto the walkway's edge. Nib looked down at him and observed, gently, 'You look worse than me.'
Nib explained the delay. They had been too far away to hear the knocks, and Minho hadn't crossed the damaged strut. Once Minho was safe, Nib had run back.
Sejin examined Taeo with her penlight. He protested that he hadn't even been inside. She answered, 'No. You were out here.'
She gave Nib water. He immediately offered it to Taeo. 'You first.' A shaky laugh finally escaped Taeo as he looked at the bottle.
Minho, the crewman, and the mule returned dusty but unhurt. The strut and its prop had fallen behind Minho, blocking the bend. Their survey was complete.
Minho blamed Nib's trip under the cracked support for a new white hair. Nib accepted the credit with a perfectly straight 'You're welcome.'
Haein studied the frame. Knocks crossed but couldn't carry far enough. Perhaps a cable could carry the radio signal. Minho's first request was a price.
Minho promised to credit Nib for spotting the crack in the survey report. Nib specified the name he wanted recorded: just Nib.
That night, Nib counted his full sixty-thousand-won payment for forty-three minutes inside. Taeo explained day rates. Nib announced that he liked them.
He placed the white pebble on his drawing, filling the blank outline beside the path below his old watch post.
Taeo asked whether that meant home was close. Nib allowed only what he knew: the stone matched. He made no bigger claim.
A late-news alert interrupted them. A porter was missing after a Dokgo Contracting job in Guro. Taeo opened the report.
The missing worker was in his sixties. Outside the construction site, other porters stood behind a cordon while violet gate light showed beyond the hoarding.
Nib asked whether porter meant something like the wooden mule. Taeo's answer was tired and serious. This was a human porter.
The news showed a young woman crying, clutching her hard hat and staring at the chained entrance. The reporter gave Dokgo's explanation: the man had left voluntarily.
